title: Gradient descent, distributions and sampling
subtitle: The four mathematical ideas behind almost every model: optimise by following the slope, describe uncertainty with distributions, and trust averages.

vec.title: Vectors, matrices, dot products
vec.body: A row of a table is a vector; the table is a matrix X (rows = examples, columns = features). The dot product w·x = Σwᵢxᵢ is a weighted sum — the heart of linear models and neurons. Matrix product Xw scores every row at once. Distance ‖a − b‖ measures similarity.

deriv.title: Derivatives and the gradient
deriv.body: f′(x) is the slope; it points uphill. For several variables the gradient ∇f collects partial derivatives and points in the steepest-ascent direction. To minimise a loss, walk the opposite way. At a minimum the gradient is zero.

gd.title: Gradient descent
gd.body: Repeat x ← x − η f′(x), with learning rate η. For f = x² − 4x + 5 (minimum at x = 2) and η = 0.2 from x = −1, after 15 steps x = 1.99859. With η = 1.1 the steps overshoot more than they correct and it oscillates. Too small is slow; too large is unstable.

dist.title: Distributions
dist.body: A distribution assigns probabilities to outcomes. Binomial counts successes in n trials; Poisson counts events per interval; the normal N(μ, σ²) models measurement noise. About 95 % of a normal lies within ±1.96σ: here P = 0.95. Standardise z = (x − μ)/σ to compare different scales.

clt.title: Sampling and the central limit theorem
clt.body: Means of samples of size n are roughly normal with standard error σ/√n, whatever the population. Simulated means of 30 from a skewed exponential population have sd 0.184 versus theory 0.183.

ci.title: Confidence intervals
ci.body: x̄ ± 1.96σ/√n is a 95 % interval. In 40 simulated studies 97.5% of intervals caught the true mean, with half-width 3.92.
